# Research question

**Research question:**

Among adults aged 60 to 75 in primary care diagnosed with COPD, does **smoking status** have any association with how far they are able walk within 6 minutes measured at baseline and six times more over 6 months, taking into account their usual **level of physical activity**?

> It would be beneficial to understand whether there is a pattern in how far the participants are able to walk within 6 minutes during each follow up depending on their smoking status and whether their usual **level of physical activity** also affects the distance they are able to walk. If there is, then a further analysis into how much it affects and whether a baseline for each permutation exists by finding their means and standard deviation (or median and IQR), followed up with knowing if a progression or even regression exists at each follow-up. It is worth knowing the relationships between these exposures as it could serve as a promoting point for avoiding smoking as well as having a better physical activity level despite having COPD. An initial assumption around this research question is that active smokers should have a lower distance walked in 6 minutes while participants with higher level of physical activity should have higher distance walked. However, the following analyses will prove or disprove this hypothesis.

# Data import and structure

```{r import}
# Baseline data
baseline = read.table('data/Baseline_Data.tsv', header = TRUE, sep = '\t')
str(baseline)
summary(baseline)

# Visits data
visits = read.table('data/Visits_Data.tsv', header = TRUE, sep = '\t')
str(visits)
summary(visits)
visits_per_id = aggregate(visit ~ ID, data = visits, FUN = length)
unique(visits_per_id$visit)
nrow(visits_per_id[visits_per_id$visit == 7, ])
nrow(visits_per_id[visits_per_id$visit == 6, ])
```

The baseline data contains 501 rows of data with 10 columns (variables). Some of the data types from the baseline data are not automatically the correct data type according to the dictionary and also contain some NA values. Possible duplicate ID shown from the baseline summary with 501 observations but only 500 unique values. The visits data contains 3466 rows of data with 3 columns (variables), each participants are expected to have 7 visits total but 20 participants only have 6 visits while 478 participants have the full 7 visits.

# Data quality assessment and cleaning

## Baseline data

```{r clean-baseline}
# Duplicates
baseline[duplicated(baseline$ID), 'ID']
baseline[baseline$ID == 'COPD000078', ] # Exact same row, index 78 and 501

# Factor columns: sex, smoker, phy_activity, diabetes, ethnicity, inhaler
# Sex
unique(baseline$sex)
baseline[baseline$sex == 12, ] # 1 row

# Smoker
unique(baseline$smoker)
baseline[baseline$smoker == -999, ] # 3 rows

# phy_activity
unique(baseline$phy_activity)
baseline[baseline$phy_activity == 'Hihg' &
    !is.na(baseline$phy_activity), ] # 6 rows; Typo 'Hihg'

# Diabetes
unique(baseline$diabetes) # No issues

# Ethnicity
unique(baseline$ethnicity)
baseline[baseline$ethnicity == 4 &
    !is.na(baseline$ethnicity), -1] # 4 rows; Unclear error

# Inhaler
unique(baseline$inhaler) # No issues

# Numerical / continuous columns: age, bmi
numerical_baseline_cols = c('age', 'bmi')
summary(baseline[, numerical_baseline_cols])

# BMI
head(baseline[order(baseline$bmi, decreasing = TRUE),
    c('ID', 'bmi')]) # Irregular BMI values of 288.0, 295.0

# Exacerbations
unique(baseline$exacerbations) # No issues

# Handling data issues
baseline = baseline[-501, ] # Duplicate
baseline$sex[baseline$sex == 12] = NA  # Sex
baseline$smoker[baseline$smoker == -999] = NA # Smoker
baseline$phy_activity[baseline$phy_activity == 'Hihg'] = 'High' # Physical activity
baseline$ethnicity[baseline$ethnicity == 4] = NA  # Ethnicity
baseline$bmi[baseline$bmi == 288 | baseline$bmi == 295] = NA # BMI

# Factor type of each categorical variables as new variables
baseline$fsex = factor(baseline$sex, levels = c(1, 2),
    labels = c('Female', 'Male')
)
baseline$fsmoker = factor(baseline$smoker, levels = c(0, 1, 2),
    labels = c('Never smoked', 'Ex smoker', 'Current smoker')
)
baseline$fphy_activity = factor(baseline$phy_activity,
    labels = c('Low', 'Moderate', 'High', 'Very_high')
)
baseline$fdiabetes = factor(baseline$diabetes, levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c('No', 'Yes')
)
baseline$fethnicity = factor(baseline$ethnicity, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
    labels = c('Group1', 'Group2', 'Group3')
)
baseline$finhaler = factor(baseline$inhaler, levels = c(0, 1),
    labels = c('Not receiving inhaler', 'Receiving inhaler')
)
```

## Visits data

```{r clean-visits}
str(visits)
visits[duplicated(visits), ] # No full duplicates
visits[duplicated(visits[, c('ID', 'visit')]),
    c('ID', 'visit')] # No duplicates by ID and visit

visits$fvisit = factor(visits$visit, levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
    labels = c('Baseline', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6')
)
```

| 3 | baseline, smoker | Value of `-999` found | `unique(baseline$smoker)` shows the unique values of smoker | Clear error | Update values to `NA` | By convention the value `-999` is typically used to denote missing data | 3 rows |
| 4 | baseline, phy_activity | Label `Hihg` found | `unique(baseline$phy_activity)` shows the unique values of phy_activity | Uncertain value | Update label to `High` | The typo is obvious where instead of `High`, the label `Hihg` was given | 6 rows |

| 7 | baseline; sex, smoker, phy_activity, diabetes, ethnicity, inhaler | Wrong data type | `str(baseline)` shows the data type | Wrong data type | Cast to factor as a new corresponding variable prefixed with `f` | The data type is casted to factor following the data dictionary | All rows |

# Missing data

## Baseline data

```{r missing-baseline, include = FALSE}
# Baseline
colSums(is.na(baseline))

# Smoker
baseline[is.na(baseline$smoker), -1] # No clear pattern

# Physical activity
baseline[is.na(baseline$phy_activity), -1] # No clear pattern

# Diabetes
baseline[is.na(baseline$diabetes), -1] # No clear pattern

# Ethnicity
baseline[is.na(baseline$ethnicity), -1] # No clear pattern
```

Missing data in the baseline data occured in the variables: **smoking status, usual level of physical activity, diabetes status, and ethnicity** with not very clear patterns on the missingness

| Variable | Total missing | Pattern | Type of missing |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| Smoking status | 3 rows | Too little data to find any missing patterns | Missing completely at random |
| Usual level of physical activity | 14 rows | Majority of the missing occurred are participants ex smokers, but not enough data to conclude a confident pattern | Missing completely at random |
| Diabetes | 10 rows | Majority of the missing occurred are participants receiving inhaler, but not enough data to conclude a confident pattern | Missing completely at random |
| Ethnicity | 16 rows | Majority of the missing occurred are participants without diabetes, but not enough data to conclude a confident pattern | Missing completely at random |

All the variables with missing data are presumed to be missing completely at random because while the majority of the missing data occurred on patients receiving inhaler, there is not enough data to draw a clear pattern.

## Visits data

```{r missing-visits}
colSums(is.na(visits))
kable(table(visits[is.na(visits$walk6min), 'visit']), col.names = c('Visit', 'Total NA'), align = 'l')

invalid_participants = visits[which(visits$visit == 0 & is.na(visits$walk6min)), 'ID']

nrow(visits[visits$ID %in% invalid_participants, ]) # Total rows with missing baseline measures

# Exclude all participants with no baseline measure
valid_visits = visits[!visits$ID %in% invalid_participants, ]
nrow(valid_visits) # 3298 rows left in the visits data
```

Some missing follow-up data is expected and could possibly be because of lost to follow-up. However, missing baseline measure should not happen as it should have been done on enrolment. Moving on with the analysis, participants with missing baseline will be excluded as they may be invalid participants. The total data excluded is only 168 rows or around 1% which would not have a significant impact on the analysis. For the participants without missing baseline but missing follow-up they will still be analysed but only including the valid follow-ups (not NA). Furthermore, attrition grew slightly over the course of the follow-ups with the most lost happening at the fifth follow up at 43 missing, followed with the last follow up at 35 missing. The rest of the follow-ups had mostly around 24 lost to follow-ups. The total data left after excluding this data is 3298 rows.

# Data linkage

Since baseline data has 500 rows of data and visits had 3298 rows of data post data cleaning, after merging there should be 3298 rows of data assuming both datasets contains the same unique participant IDs.

```{r linkage}
linked_data = merge(baseline, valid_visits, by = 'ID',
    all.x = FALSE, all.y = FALSE
)
nrow(linked_data)
```

The total dataset after merging is 3298 rows. **Inner join** is used here because only participants that had their demographic characteristics and exposures taken as well as their outcome measures are needed for the analysis. Participants that had their demographic characteristics and exposures measured but do not have any baseline or outcome measures (or vice versa, patients that have a baseline or outcome measures but don't exist in the demographic characteristics and exposures dataset) are excluded and treated as invalid participants. The merged dataset now contains the participant information, characteristics such as pre-existing conditions or exposures, as well as their baseline measure and all their follow-ups.

# Exploratory analysis and visualisation

## Exposure characteristics

```{r frequency-smoker, tab.cap = 'Total participants for each smoking status'}
total_smokers = as.data.frame(table(baseline$fsmoker))
total_smokers$total_pct = round(total_smokers$Freq / sum(total_smokers$Freq) * 100, 1)
kable(total_smokers, align = 'l',
    col.names = c('Smoking status', 'Total participants (n)', 'Total participants (%)')
)
```

370 of the participants or 74.4% are ex smokers, followed with 87 current smokers or 17.5%, and 4 who never smoked or 8% of the participants.

```{r frequency-phyactivity, tab.cap = 'Total participants for each level of physical activity'}
total_activity = as.data.frame(table(baseline$fphy_activity))
total_activity$total_pct = round(total_activity$Freq / sum(total_activity$Freq) * 100, 1)
kable(total_activity, align = 'l',
    col.names = c('Level of physical activity', 'Total participants (n)', 'Total participants (%)')
)
```

The majority of the participants have low physical activity level with 37%, then high level of physical activity with 29.8%, followed with moderate level of physical activity or 19.1%, and the least frequent is participants who have very high level of physical activity with only 14%.

```{r frequency-smoker-activity, tab.cap = 'Crosstabulation of smoker status and level of physical activity'}
total_smoker_activity = as.data.frame(table(baseline[, c('fsmoker', 'fphy_activity')]))

pct_within_smoker = round(
    prop.table(
        table(baseline[, c('fsmoker', 'fphy_activity')]), margin = 1
    ) * 100, 2
) # Fetch the percentage within smokers

pct_within_activity = round(
    prop.table(
        table(baseline[, c('fsmoker', 'fphy_activity')]), margin = 2
    ) * 100, 2
) # Fetch the percentage within activity level

# Build percentage columns
total_smoker_activity$pct_within_smoker = c(pct_within_smoker)
total_smoker_activity$pct_within_activity = c(pct_within_activity)
total_smoker_activity$pct_total = round(total_smoker_activity$Freq / sum(total_smoker_activity$Freq) * 100, 2)

# Build formatted table
total_smoker_activity$row_col_pct = sprintf('%d (%.2f) (%.2f)', total_smoker_activity$Freq, 
    total_smoker_activity$pct_within_smoker, total_smoker_activity$pct_within_activity
)

total_smoker_activity$freq_row_pct = sprintf('%d (%.2f)', total_smoker_activity$Freq, total_smoker_activity$pct_within_smoker)

kable(total_smoker_activity[, c('fsmoker', 'fphy_activity', 'row_col_pct', 'pct_total')], 
    align = 'l',
    col.names = c('Smoking status', 'Level of physical activity', 
                  'Participants, <br> n (within smoker type, %) (within physical activity, %)', 
                  'Total %')
)
```


```{r heatmap-smoking-physical, fig.cap = 'Heatmap of smoking status and level of physical activity'}
ggplot(data = total_smoker_activity, aes(fsmoker, fphy_activity, fill = pct_within_smoker)) +
    geom_tile(colour = 'white', linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = freq_row_pct,
            colour = ifelse(pct_within_smoker > 20, 'white', 'black')
        ),
        fontface = 'bold',
        size = 3,
        show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
        option = 'C',
        direction = -1,
        name = 'Within smoking status,\nn (%)'
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(
        values = c('white' = '#FFFFFF', 'black' = '#111111')
    ) +
    labs(
        x = 'Smoking status',
        y = 'Level of physical activity',
        title = 'Heatmap of cross tabulation between smoking status \n and level of physical activity'
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.box.background = element_rect(
            fill = alpha('#e5e5e5', 1), linewidth = 0.2, linetype = "solid", color = "#222222"
        )
    )
```

In those who never smoked and the ex smoker groups, the trends are the same where the majority have a low level of physical activity with 42.11% and 36.57% respectively, followed with high level of physical activity at 31.58% and 30.19%, then moderate levels at 18.42% and 19.67%, and the least populated with very high level of physical activity at 7.89% and 13.57%. However, for current smokers the trend is slightly different where instead of very high level of physical activity being the least frequent, it is swapped with moderate level of physical activity instead.

## Outcome characteristics

```{r distance-per-visit, fig.cap = 'Distance walked in 6 minutes per visit'}
overall_mean = mean(linked_data$walk6min, na.rm = TRUE)
ggplot(
      data = linked_data[!is.na(linked_data$walk6min), 
      c('walk6min', 'fvisit')], 
      aes(x = fvisit, y = walk6min, fill = fvisit)
    ) +
    geom_violin() +
    geom_jitter(
      alpha = 0.25, size = 0.4, 
      width = 0.1, colour = '#1A1A1A',
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      aes(yintercept = overall_mean, linetype ='Overall mean'), 
      linewidth = 0.8, colour = '#444444'
    ) +
    stat_summary(# 1 SD
      fun = mean, 
      fun.min = function(y) mean(y) - sd(y),
      fun.max = function(y) mean(y) + sd(y),
      geom = 'errorbar', colour = '#FFFFFF',
      width = 0.1, linewidth = 0.8,
    ) +
    stat_summary(# Group mean
      fun = mean, geom = 'point',
      colour = '#FFFFFF', size = 2.5,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(200, 600), breaks = c(seq(200, 600, 100), round(overall_mean))) +
    scale_linetype_manual(
      name = '',
      values = c('Overall mean' = 'dashed')
    ) +
    scale_fill_discrete(guide = 'none') +
    labs(
        x = 'Visit',
        y = 'Distance walked in 6 minutes (m)',
        title = 'Distance walked in 6 minutes per visit',
        fill = 'Visit'
    ) + 
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm")
    )
```

Across all the visits including baseline, the distribution of how far the participants are able to walk in 6 minutes across the baseline and all the follow-ups are similar and approximately normal with a few outliers but not notable. The mean and 1 standard deviation spread as noted by the white error bar within each violin is relatively similar. Overall, without accounting for any specific exposures, there is no growth in the distance the participants are able to walk in 6 minutes from the baseline to the follow-ups.

```{r distance-means-spread, tab.cap = 'Summary statistics of 6 minute walk distance without specific exposure'}
distance_means = aggregate(
    walk6min ~ fvisit, data = linked_data,
    FUN = function(x) round(mean(x), 2)
)
distance_sd = aggregate(
    walk6min ~ fvisit, data = linked_data,
    FUN = function(x) round(sd(x), 2)
)

distance_summary = merge(
    distance_means, distance_sd, 
    by = 'fvisit'
)
distance_summary$one_sd_spread = sprintf('%.2f, %.2f', 
    distance_summary$walk6min.x - distance_summary$walk6min.y,
    distance_summary$walk6min.x + distance_summary$walk6min.y
)

kable(distance_summary[order(distance_summary$fvisit),],
    align = 'l',
    col.names = c('Visit', 'Average 6 minutes <br>walk distance (m)', 
                  'Standard deviation 6 <br>minutes walk distance (m)',
                  'Mean ± 1 SD'),
    row.names = FALSE
)
```

The table above shows how similar the average and the spread of the data is between the baseline and the follow-ups. It also further shows in detail the absence of growth from the baseline to the follow-ups. The highest average occurred on the second follow up but the increase from the baseline is only by 0.48 metres, while the baseline against all the other follow-ups only decreased. The lowest average is on the last follow-up at 378.20 metres, almost 3 metres lower than the baseline.

```{r setup-analysis-df}
# Subset dataframe to only include variables of interest and exclude NA values
analysis_df = subset(linked_data, 
     !is.na(walk6min) & (
       !is.na(fsmoker) |
       !is.na(fphy_activity)
     ),
     select = c(fsmoker, fphy_activity, fvisit, walk6min)
)
```


### Univariate analysis

<a id="univariate-smoker-setup"></a>
```{r univariate-smoker-setup}
smoker_outcome_plot = function(smoking_status) {
    # Filter dataframe
    df = analysis_df[analysis_df$fsmoker == smoking_status & !is.na(analysis_df$fsmoker), ]
    # Fetch the mean within the filtered smoker group
    within_group_mean = round(mean(df$walk6min))
    
    # Build the graph
    ggplot(
        data = df,
        aes(x = fsmoker, y = walk6min, fill = fvisit)
    ) +
    geom_violin(width = 0.85) +
    geom_hline(
      aes(yintercept = within_group_mean, linetype ='Within group mean'), 
      linewidth = 0.8, colour = '#444444'
    ) +
    stat_summary(# Within smoking and visit mean
      fun = mean, geom = 'point',
      colour = '#FFFFFF', size = 1.5,
      show.legend = FALSE, position = position_dodge(width = 0.85)
    ) +
    scale_linetype_manual(
      name = '',
      values = c('Within group mean' = 'dashed')
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        limits = c(200, 600), 
        breaks = c(seq(200, 600, 100), within_group_mean)
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c('#E69F00', '#56B4E9', '#009E73', '#F0E442', '#0072B2', '#D55E00', '#CC79A7')) +
    labs(
        x = 'Smoking status',
        y = 'Distance walked in 6 minutes (m)',
        fill = 'Visit'
    ) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(
      legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm")
    )
}
```

```{r univariate-smoker, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 8}
never_smoked = smoker_outcome_plot('Never smoked')
ex_smoker = smoker_outcome_plot('Ex smoker')
current_smoker = smoker_outcome_plot('Current smoker')

never_smoked / ex_smoker / current_smoker +
    plot_layout(
        guides = 'collect',
        axis_titles = 'collect'
    ) +
    plot_annotation(
        title = 'Distance walked in 6 minutes per visit per smoking status',
        theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
    )
```

Taking into account the participants' smoking status, it is clear that current smokers has a far lower 6 minutes walk distance average at each visit as well as the overall average compared to ex smokers and those who never smoked. Those who never smoked and ex smokers have very similar averages across all the visits. However, the shape of the violins for those who never smoked and ex smokers are different. Those who never smoked tend to be wider above the group mean, while ex smokers tend to be wider below the group mean.

## Limitations

Potential limitation: 

- Study participants limited to 60-75 years old 
- No statistical test means can't conclude a result with statistical significance 
- No regression model means can't quantify magnitude of predictor against the dependent variable
- Potential confounders
